title: Words Follow a Letter Pattern
statement:
You get a pattern of lowercase letters and a sentence s of lowercase words separated by single spaces. Return true if the sentence follows the pattern.

Following the pattern means there are exactly as many words as letters, and you can pair letters with words one to one: every copy of a letter stands for the same word, and two different letters never stand for the same word.

examples.why: x is always "red" and y is always "blue".
Each letter on its own is consistent, but x and y would both mean "red". The pairing must work in both directions.
Three letters but only two words.

constraints: s has no leading or trailing spaces and words are separated by one space
hints: First split the sentence into words. When can you answer false without looking at any letter?
Walk letters and words side by side and remember what each letter has meant so far. Is that enough to catch "xyyx" against four copies of "red"?
Keep two maps, letter → word and word → letter. At each position, if either map already holds a different partner, the answer is false.

explain.intuition:
The rule is a one-to-one pairing, so it has to be checked from both sides. A single map from letter to word catches a letter that changes its meaning, but not two letters that share a word. A second map from word to letter catches that.

Another view: write each sequence as "where did this item first appear". "xyyx" becomes 0 1 1 0, and "red blue blue red" also becomes 0 1 1 0. The sentence follows the pattern exactly when both sequences have the same shape.
steps: Split s on spaces. If the word count differs from pattern.length, return false.
Walk index i with letter c and word w.
If c is mapped to something other than w, or w is mapped to something other than c, return false.
Otherwise record both directions and continue. Return true at the end.
pitfalls: Checking only letter → word. Then "xy" against "red red" wrongly passes.
Forgetting the length check, so a pattern of 3 letters matches the first 3 of 4 words.
Using a plain object as the word map. Words like constructor already exist on {}; use Map or Object.create(null).

solutions.title: Two maps, both directions
solutions.idea: Map letter → word and word → letter, and reject any position where an existing partner disagrees.

solutions.title: Compare first-appearance shapes
solutions.idea: Replace every item by the index where it first appeared. The two sequences must come out identical.

followups: Now the sentence has no spaces and each letter may stand for any non-empty substring. How would you search for a pairing?
Group a list of sentences into classes that follow the same pattern. What key would you hash?
